book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal

chapters.relation: Vannatta's introduction frames the volume with a traffic-intersection metaphor: Klosterman's campaign against the phrase 'guilty pleasure' questions whether the one-way roads of high and low culture are real at all, and the contributors deliberately violate the traffic rules (Kierkegaard meets KISS, Baudrillard meets Britney Spears). It reads Klosterman's line that 'nothing is ever in and of itself' through Kant's noumena-phenomena distinction: like Kant's knowing subject, we never reach the in-itself but only perspectives refracted through rock bands, sports teams, and TV. The introduction presents the Guns N' Roses tribute band Paradise City (identity effaced to imitate an equally constructed identity) and the rock-death road trip of Killing Yourself to Live as Klosterman's way of recovering authenticity, arguing that living with the possibility of one's own death is more authentic than fleeing it.

Auxier argues that Klosterman's signature lists always carry an 'immanent order' of value, illustrated by the twenty-two teenagers' simultaneous classroom thoughts in Downtown Owl and his own contested ranking of the five greatest rock bands. He reads the seventeen-page sober conversation between Julia and Vance, printed with 'what she meant' and 'what he meant' under each remark, through Kant's extensive versus intensive magnitudes: the spoken words are an extensive whole, but the multiple unshared perspectives form an intensive whole no list can exhaust, which is why philosophers crave the 'tug of necessity' that intensive relations never deliver. Plato's Leontius, who rubbernecked at corpses despite his disgust, explains both Klosterman's TMI confessions in Killing Yourself to Live and the 'recoil of the shit-canon' by which we learn to order our desires, while Julia's carbon-monoxide death in the blizzard shows the world converting intensive possibilities into extensive necessity.

Vannatta explains why Seinfeld reruns now fall flat through Klosterman's neologism 'unironically': since about 1991 irony has become the invisible background of American comedy, a pervasive detachment that David Foster Wallace named and that Jedediah Purdy's For Common Things attacks as the gap between phenomenon and essence. Against Purdy's ironist (Seinfeld's Jerry, mastered by irony, believing in nothing but his own interests), the chapter sets Kierkegaard's Socrates, whose 'infinite absolute negativity' and confessing ignorance serve a truth he cannot define, and asks whether Klosterman, probing the gap between Bono's rehearsed car-ride persona and his inner self, is master of irony or mastered by it. The answer places Chuck midway between the two jailed ironists, Socrates and the Seinfeld finale: like Socrates he knows his own ignorance and serves the undefined idea of self-understanding, but only through pop-culture resemblance (KISS where Jerry used Superman), unable to master irony any more than he can bite his own teeth.

Reisch rebuts Klosterman's Esquire claim that culture, unlike people and movements, can never be wrong because no larger framework stands outside it: he argues something can also go wrong relative to its own internal values, betraying itself as a self-sabotaging painter does. His exhibit is Phil Collins's 'In the Air Tonight', scored by a jokey 'popular music vapidity index' that divides emotional drama by lyrical substance, on which Springsteen's 'Born in the U.S.A.' rates near a healthy 1 while Collins's operatic anguish over a contentless 'it' divides by zero and becomes infinitely vapid. Since the song is beloved cultural wallpaper, its awfulness shows that culture as a whole can betray itself and its members, which is why serious fans feel genuinely let down by hit movies and best-seller lists.

Curko and Greguric read Klosterman's glam-rock fandom as a problem of identity and masks: Nietzsche's Apollonian-Dionysian split casts Chuck as a self-controlled Apollonian writing about Dionysian excess in Guns N' Roses, Motley Crue, and Whitesnake, while Descartes's remark that actors wear masks to hide their shame introduces the tribute band Paradise City, a 'real copy' whose members would have no personalities left if they fully succeeded. The authors extend the mask question to Facebook and online avatars, where media saturation makes us 'copies without the original' and identity stops being self-same. They end by crowning Klosterman a modern Socrates of 'Know thyself' and a Stoic exemplar: admire your heroes like Satriani but do not steal their identities, control what you can (never your reputation or your time of death), and keep daring the endless search for self-knowledge.

Vannatta starts from Klosterman's confession that his first dates run on three and a half dates' worth of contrived material, and asks how self-knowledge is possible at all if, as Errol Morris tells Klosterman, we have no privileged access to our own minds. After a tour through Descartes's cogito, Kant's unity of apperception, Freud's unconscious, and Foucault's discourse-constructed subject, the chapter argues with Foucault's Ramist logic of similarity that Klosterman's thought really works by resemblance, mapping his exes onto members of KISS and hearing a dead friend in every Replacements song. Heidegger supplies the resolution: thrown into the crowd's world, we recover ourselves only through its inauthentic pop culture, and Klosterman's 'living is dying, little by little' and obsessive rock-death writing enact being-toward-death as the condition of authenticity.

Rood unpacks Klosterman's 'This Is Emo' thesis that no woman will ever satisfy him: women love Lloyd Dobler rather than John Cusack, and everyone measures real relationships against Hollywood fake love (Coldplay songs, the Woody Allen Personality Type) until, as Klosterman puts it, real people actively trying to live like fake people are no less fake. He reads this through Sartre's cafe waiter and Butler's gender performativity to argue identity is learned performance, and through Plato's cave updated to a reclining-seat movie theater where we mistake projected shadows for real love. The deepest diagnosis is Baudrillard's hyperreal, glossed as a social-constructionist rerun of Kant's Copernican revolution, against which Rood's own objection lands: Klosterman covertly assumes a pure unmediated self that cannot exist, so the answer to fake love is not escape from mediation but self-control within it.

Sienkiewicz takes Klosterman's hyperthetical of a crystal ball showing an unchangeable future in which you are blissfully obsessed with CFL football as a secular version of the traditional Jewish and Christian problem of divine foreknowledge versus human freedom. He offers the 'movie' solution: as when watching the chest-wax scene in The 40-Year-Old Virgin, a vantage point outside the event's time (God's, or yours before the fixed future) can behold it without having scripted it, so foreknowledge and free will remain logically compatible. Since we already live toward the one absolutely certain future, our own deaths, the portal should change nothing about how you act, though you still should not watch a league that plays with only three downs.

Flanders reads Killing Yourself to Live as asking whether dying can be good for the person who dies: Jeff Buckley's 'Hallelujah' and Kurt Cobain's myth became deeper and more successful only after the fact, as if death were a career move. He answers with Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, where the fortunes of descendants can affect the happiness of the dead: our life-stories outlive their authors, so fans' posthumous devotion can really benefit Buckley, though no posthumous fame can add virtue that was never lived (Michael Jackson's rehabilitation cannot touch how he actually lived). Klosterman's road trip ultimately undercuts the question: the earnest Great White concert mourners remember what truly was there, while Cobain's fans retroactively invent meaning to gain 'credibility by mourning retrospectively', so worshipping the rock dead manufactures an inauthentic afterlife, and Klosterman must kill the unserious fan in himself to live.

Brittingham reads Klosterman's celebrity interviews through Kierkegaard's The Sickness unto Death, taking the self as a synthesis of the immediate and the symbolic, finite and infinite. Britney Spears, who claims never to have thought about the sexual iconography behind her curtain, embodies the despair of ignorance in not knowing one has a self; Bono, embarrassed by his messianic 1980s posturing and wishing to shed that iconic self while remaining 'self-conscious about being self-conscious', embodies despair at not willing to be oneself; Metallica's Some Kind of Monster breakdown, with rehab, a hired therapist, and Kirk Hammett dreading having to take out the trash, embodies defiant despair, the 'king without a country' who would be absolute master of himself. Jeff Tweedy's uncool acceptance of both his suburban dad-life and his silly symbolic persona, plus Kierkegaard's remedy of resting transparently in the power that established us, mark the only way to be 'for real' rather than full of shit.

Vosen confesses her own case of Klosterman's fake-love thesis, hundreds of viewings of Say Anything for Lloyd Dobler and his boom box, and accepts that everyone from Huxtable-watching parents to Real World casting wants Hollywood love and one-dimensional archetypes. Her framework is Bakhtin's carnival: Sex, Drugs, and Cocoa Puffs is carnivalesque literature that suspends cultural hierarchies (thirty million Americans of every class watching American Idol), crowns low culture like Pamela Anderson and Saved by the Bell, and makes Klosterman both carnie and king through his self-awareness. The dark twist is Klosterman's Real World point that we sacrifice our complicated personalities to play flat archetypes like Puck because communication becomes easier, 'we must kill ourselves... in order to live', and knowing it, as Klosterman does, wins the crown without granting immunity.

Priebe answers Klosterman's dream-VCR hyperthetical, would you tape your dreams knowing family and closest friends must watch along, with an enthusiastic yes, defining dreams as mini-movies directed by the unconscious with a nod to Freud's repressed thoughts and Jung's dream symbols, and arguing that lucid control would let her censor or spice the footage mid-dream. She pitches the device as entertainment gold, surreal dreams, post-drinking dreams better than reality television, and nightmare reels her sister could buy, plus an intimacy bonus: after watching, friends and family would finally understand her eccentricities. The punchline is that she does not dream eighty-five percent of the time, so her tapes would cure insomnia rather than scandalize anyone.

Sienkiewicz argues that Klosterman's LeBron James 'Decision' episode on Bill Simmons's B.S. Report modeled genuine public-sphere deliberation: where ESPN's Skip Bayless scored points over whether James looked remorseful, Klosterman proposed, via Tupac's 'Only God can judge me', that the televised announcement was a statement of confidence and a refusal to play the one-dimensional reality-TV role America demanded. The chapter lays out Habermas's eighteenth-century public sphere, its salons and 'public sphere of letters' where low-stakes aesthetic arguments (Mozart then, the Guns N' Roses tribute band Paradise City now) train disinterested rational debate, and concedes Habermas's golden age is idealized historical fiction much like a Klosterman hyperthetical. Though Habermas blames commercial media for corroding rational discourse, Sienkiewicz contends that long-form podcasts like The B.S. Report and Contexts give Klosterman's pop-culture arguments the time and independence the old salons had, so arguing about Billy Joel or Ace Frehley strengthens rather than absolves democratic culture.

holes.name: Intensive vs. Extensive Magnitude
holes.what: Kant's distinction between extensive magnitude, a whole whose parts add up to it exactly like a hundred pennies making a dollar, and intensive magnitude, a degree of reality that every real thing has and whose partial perspectives never exhaust the whole.
holes.why: Chapter 9 builds its entire reading of Klosterman's lists and the three-perspective Julia/Vance dialogue in Downtown Owl on this distinction, and no existing taxonomy concept covers it.

holes.name: Mikhail Bakhtin
holes.what: Russian thinker of dialogism and the carnivalesque: literature and popular festivities that suspend official hierarchies, crown and decrown kings, and celebrate low culture against official seriousness.
holes.why: Chapter 20's entire framework reads Sex, Drugs, and Cocoa Puffs as carnivalesque literature, with Klosterman as the crowned and dethroned carnival king, and the taxonomy has no Bakhtin slug.

holes.name: The Carnivalesque
holes.what: Bakhtin's notion that carnival forms, in festivities or in literature, temporarily invert social hierarchies and mix high and low in a liberating celebration of the subversive.
holes.why: Chapter 20 applies the carnivalesque to American Idol, Pamela Anderson, Saved by the Bell, and Klosterman's crowning as carnival king, and no existing concept slug fits this material.
